about: Labelled statement PAIRS for the forensics `edited_number` rule. Built after FINDING-2 measured 90 alert-severity findings from 20 ordinary ledger rows. Precision is what matters: this rule accuses a document of being tampered with, so a false positive is louder than a missed one.
limitations: SYNTHETIC, and the per-item-table class is deliberately over-represented — it is the class that fires.
Scores the TEXTUAL predicate only. The engine also gates on cross-FILE provenance first; FINDING-2's false positives all passed that gate legitimately, so the text is where the error is.
One annotator. 'edited' means the two statements are the SAME claim with one figure changed — not merely that they disagree, which is contradiction-core.v1's question.
Real tampering in the wild is rarer and subtler than these fixtures. High precision here is necessary, not sufficient.

cases.label: ordinary
cases.a: Item 5 for VendorCo recorded value 1000.
cases.b: Item 6 for VendorCo recorded value 1000.
cases.why: THE PRECISION HOLE THE FIX DOES NOT CLOSE. Two adjacent table rows whose only differing number is the row index. Every per-item-table case in v1 differs in two or four positions, so a one-differing-number row was never tested and a fix tuned to 'exactly one number changed' passes the v1 dataset while still accusing this shape. Recorded as a known false positive rather than discovered later in production.

cases.label: edited
cases.a: Payment of 250000 was received on 2026-03-04.
cases.b: Payment of 750000 was received on 2026-09-04.
cases.why: THE RECALL COST OF THE FIX, stated up front. A doctored payment where both the amount and the date moved. All eight genuine cases in v1 change exactly one number, so 'exactly one' scored a perfect 1.000 against a dataset that could not contradict it. This case can, and it is expected to FAIL after the fix.

cases.label: edited
cases.a: Acme holds 34 percent worth 500000 dollars.
cases.b: Acme holds 51 percent worth 900000 dollars.
cases.why: Second multi-number doctoring, so the recall cost is a measured rate rather than a single anecdote that could be dismissed as unrepresentative.

cases.label: edited
cases.a: The retainer was 24000 per quarter.
cases.b: The retainer was 96000 per quarter.
cases.why: CONTROL for the two cases above: a single-number doctoring in the same money shape. If this fails alongside them the fix broke the main path; if it passes, the loss is specifically multi-number edits and nothing wider.

cases.label: ordinary
cases.a: Section 3 of the agreement covers indemnity.
cases.b: Section 4 of the agreement covers indemnity.
cases.why: SECOND instance of the e030 hole, in a different surface — section numbering rather than table rows. Included even though it FAILS, because one failing case can be dismissed as unrepresentative and two make the residual hole a rate. Structural numbering that increments is common in contracts, so this shape will occur in real documents.

cases.label: ordinary
cases.a: The agreed fee is 500000 payable on completion.
cases.b: The agreed fee is 500000, payable upon completion.
cases.why: Same figure, reworded. Originally filed as `restatement`, which was wrong: an existing dataset invariant defines restatement as a===b — identical text is corroboration, not a reworded twin. The shape gate is what must reject this pair, so `different-shape` is the category that actually describes the guard it provides.

cases.label: ordinary
cases.a: The deposit of 15000 was returned in full.
cases.b: A deposit of 15000 was returned to the client.
cases.why: Same number, different sentence. Keeps the shape gate honest: the rule must require an identical mask, not merely a shared figure, or every document mentioning the same amount becomes a tampering alert.
